**Summary.** This paper analyzes quantum search algorithms on bipartite graphs using a quantum walk defined by a generalized Laplacian. The authors prove that by tuning the Laplacian via a parameter $\alpha$, the quantum walk's search time can be made to approach the theoretical optimum. This suggests the generalized Laplacian provides a powerful tool for developing faster quantum algorithms.

**Why it may be interesting.** The explicit derivation of how tuning a system parameter ($\alpha$) can push a quantum walk towards an optimal computational limit is highly relevant for designing robust quantum algorithms.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To prove that a quantum walk governed by a generalized Laplacian can solve a search problem on a complete bipartite graph faster than standard quantum walks.

**Main result.** The generalized Laplacian quantum walk achieves an optimal search time scaling, approaching the theoretical minimum time $t^* = rac{\pi}{2} \min \left(rac{N_1}{k_1}, rac{N_2}{k_2}ight)$ in the limit where the parameter $\alpha 	o \pm\infty$.

**Method.** The analysis involves deriving the time evolution operator for the quantum walk Hamiltonian, using asymptotic analysis, and employing perturbation theory to study the behavior as the parameter $\alpha$ becomes very large.

**Model / system.** The model is a continuous-time quantum walk on a complete bipartite graph, governed by a Hamiltonian derived from a generalized Laplacian $L_\alpha = L + \alpha D$. The evolution is tracked by analyzing the probability amplitudes at different vertex types.

**Key observables.** Success probability at marked vertices, and the optimal search runtime $t^*$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The parameter $\alpha$ (controlling the degree matrix contribution), the graph sizes ($N_1, N_2$), and the number of marked vertices ($k_1, k_2$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on asymptotic approximations, particularly for large graph sizes ($N_1, N_2$) when applying perturbation theory.

**Figures summary.** Figure 2 shows the success probability vs. time for various $\alpha$ values, demonstrating the speedup. Figure 3 illustrates the time evolution of probabilities at different vertex types for a specific case.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the quantum walk model using the generalized Laplacian, analyzes the time evolution using the Hamiltonian in a reduced basis, and derives the optimal runtime by taking limits on the parameter $\alpha$.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum walks are the quantum analogues of classical random walks or Markov chains. They are universal models of quantum computing, and they underpin a variety of quantum algorithms. We prove that a continuous-time quantum walk effected by a generalized Laplacian, which can arise in spin chains, can solve a computational problem more quickly than typical quantum walks governed by the standard Laplacian or adjacency matrix. This generalized Laplacian consists of the standard Laplacian plus a real-valued multiple of the degree matrix, and we prove that as the magnitude of the multiple of the degree matrix is increased, its corresponding quantum walk can search the complete bipartite graph with multiple marked vertices in time that approaches the optimal. This raises the potential for the generalized Laplacian quantum walk to be a useful method for developing additional faster quantum algorithms.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical note examines the generalized Bures-Wasserstein distance derived from the generalized fidelity in quantum information. The authors prove that this distance fails the Data Processing Inequality in dimensions higher than two. For the qubit case, they establish specific sufficient conditions under which the DPI holds, providing deeper insights into quantum channel characterization.

**Why it may be interesting.** The study of distance metrics and their monotonicity properties (like DPI) is fundamental in quantum information theory, especially when analyzing the robustness of quantum channels.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates whether the generalized Bures-Wasserstein distance, induced by the generalized fidelity, satisfies the Data Processing Inequality (DPI) for quantum channels.

**Main result.** The distance fails to satisfy the DPI in dimensions greater than two, but sufficient conditions for the DPI are derived for the qubit case (dimension two).

**Method.** The authors use explicit formulas for the generalized fidelity, derived using Pauli matrix representations for qubits, and construct counterexamples to test the DPI.

**Model / system.** The analysis focuses on quantum states represented by positive semi-definite matrices, particularly restricting the investigation to the qubit case (2x2 matrices).

**Key observables.** Generalized Fidelity ($F_R(P, Q)$), Squared Generalized Bures-Wasserstein Distance ($B_R(P, Q)$), and the Uhlmann fidelity ($F_U$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimension of the system ($n$), and the specific matrices defining the generalized fidelity.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis provides sufficient conditions for the qubit case, but the DPI is not settled in full generality for dimension two.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the definitions for the generalized fidelity and distance. It then proves the failure of the DPI for $n \ge 3$ using counterexamples. Finally, it derives sufficient conditions for the DPI in the qubit case and determines when the generalized fidelity reduces to the Uhlmann fidelity.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this note, we show that the generalized Bures--Wasserstein distance induced by the generalized fidelity does not satisfy the data processing inequality in dimensions greater than two. In dimension two, although we do not settle the DPI in full generality, we derive two sufficient conditions guaranteeing it by using an explicit formula for the real part of the generalized fidelity. Furthermore, we find a necessary and sufficient condition under which the generalized fidelity reduces to the Uhlmann fidelity.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proves a deep mathematical equivalence between random mixed quantum states generated by tracing out an environment and a statistical mixture called the Mai-Alquier distribution. This identification is highly valuable because it allows researchers to calculate complex quantum observables, such as purity moments and determinants, using simpler tools from the theory of Dirichlet distributions and Haar averages. It unifies the theoretical understanding of induced random mixed states.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful mathematical tool to simplify calculations in open quantum systems by mapping physical environmental tracing processes onto well-understood statistical ensembles (Dirichlet mixtures).

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper establishes an exact equivalence between random mixed states induced by tracing out an environment and a specific statistical mixture known as the Mai-Alquier (MA) distribution.

**Main result.** This equivalence allows complex calculations involving induced random mixed states (like purity moments and determinants) to be recast into manageable calculations involving Dirichlet moments and low-order Haar averages.

**Method.** The authors use properties of the Ginibre ensemble and the Gamma distribution to show that the induced state distribution matches the Dirichlet-weighted mixture distribution when the Dirichlet parameter equals the system dimension.

**Model / system.** The model involves a D-dimensional system coupled to a K-dimensional environment, prepared in a Haar-random pure global state, followed by tracing out the environment to yield the induced mixed state.

**Key observables.** Purity moments ($	ext{Tr} ho^m$), mean Hilbert-Schmidt distance between ensembles, and the determinant ($\det ho$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** D (system dimension), K (environment dimension), and the Dirichlet concentration parameter $\alpha$ (which must equal D for equivalence).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The equivalence holds under the condition that the Dirichlet concentration parameter $\alpha$ matches the system dimension $D$.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the geometric equivalence for a qubit system, showing both the MA construction (convex combination) and the induced state construction using Ginibre matrix columns leading to the same Dirichlet law.

**Paper structure.** The paper first defines the induced state via partial traces over a random environment, then derives the statistical properties showing the equivalence to the MA distribution. It then applies this equivalence to derive exact formulas for key observables like purity moments, distance, and determinants.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We establish an exact equivalence in distribution between $D$-dimensional random mixed states induced by partial traces over $K$-dimensional environments and the Mai-Alquier distribution, a mixture of $K$ independent Haar-random pure states weighted by a symmetric Dirichlet distribution. This identification recasts a class of expectation values for induced ensembles into calculations involving Dirichlet moments and low-order Haar averages on a single-system state space. As applications, we recover exact purity moments up to fourth order, derive the mean Hilbert--Schmidt distance between independent induced ensembles with possibly different environment dimensions, and obtain exact average determinants. These results provide a unified and constructive perspective on induced random mixed states and on the evaluation of quantities such as purity moments, overlaps, and determinants.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes the structure of the Italian B2B commercial network using massive invoicing data, modeling firms as nodes and transactions as weighted edges. It finds the network possesses a scale-free structure and characterizes how economic importance (centrality) is unevenly distributed among a few key firms. The findings offer quantitative insights into the underlying connectivity and vulnerabilities of the national production system.

**Why it may be interesting.** The application of complex network theory, which shares mathematical tools with statistical physics (e.g., power-law distributions, critical phenomena), to a real-world economic system provides a model for analyzing emergent collective behavior in non-physical systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper characterizes the structure of the Italian production network using comprehensive firm-to-firm commercial transaction data to derive insights into the Italian economy.

**Main result.** The network exhibits a scale-free structure, indicated by heavy-tailed distributions for buyer/seller counts and centrality measures. Furthermore, the tail exponents for buyer-side distributions are found to be lower than those for seller-side distributions.

**Method.** Network analysis techniques are employed, treating firms as nodes and invoices as weighted, directed edges. Key metrics analyzed include degree distributions, network centrality (Eigenvector, Katz, PageRank), and structural properties like assortativity.

**Model / system.** The system is the network of Italian Business-to-Business (B2B) commercial relationships, constructed from electronic invoicing data from the Italian Tax Office. Nodes are firms, and edges are weighted by the total monetary amount exchanged.

**Key observables.** Distribution of buyers/sellers per firm, network centrality measures, tail exponents of degree distributions, network density, and mean degree.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis is based on the 2019 Italian electronic invoicing data, focusing on the B2B subset of transactions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is static, and while the data coverage is comprehensive, the comparison of network metrics across different international datasets is cautioned against due to potential methodological variations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the flow of transactions between entity types, the number of firms per economic sector (NACE), and maps showing regional/sectoral variations in centrality measures. Tables compare network metrics across different countries.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the economic importance of micro-structure, details the unique B2B dataset, analyzes fundamental network statistics (scale-free, small-world), and concludes with detailed sectoral and geographical breakdowns of centrality.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present a comprehensive description of the network of Italian Business-to-Business commercial relationships, based on the universe of electronic invoices collected by the Italian Tax Office. The firm-to-firm detail of the data is exploited to describe the distribution of the numbers of buyers (customers) and sellers (suppliers) per firm, the centrality of each firm in the production network, and the average distance between firms. We characterize for the first time the firm-to-firm network describing the Italian production system, and present its geographic and sectoral breakdown. The analysis reveals heavy tailed distributions for the numbers of buyers and sellers per firm, implying a scale-free structure of the network. The distributions of centrality values display heavy tails as well, indicating a strong concentration of importance in a relatively small number of firms. We estimate the tail exponents for all these distributions, finding in all cases lower exponents for downstream (buyer-side) distributions than for the upstream (seller-side) ones.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper calculates the noise threshold for fault-tolerant fermionic quantum computation using a specific non-Gaussian gate set. By analyzing the channel's structure via Uhlmann-Wootters concurrences, the authors establish a new, high upper bound of approximately 62% for the tolerable noise level. This result is crucial for designing robust quantum hardware based on fermionic physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous application of entanglement measures (concurrences) to diagnose the breakdown of non-Gaussianity in fermionic systems provides a powerful theoretical tool for assessing hardware viability in quantum computation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to determine the maximum noise level a quantum circuit can tolerate while remaining fault-tolerant for fermionic quantum computation.

**Main result.** The upper bound limit for fermionic quantum computing using the matchgate set is found to be approximately 62%, which is independent of circuit depth.

**Method.** The authors use Uhlmann-Wootters concurrences applied to the fermionic Choi state to test when the combined channel becomes 'convex Gaussian,' signaling a loss of non-Gaussian support.

**Model / system.** The system is fermionic quantum computing, which utilizes the matchgate with a non-Gaussian resource universal gate set. The analysis incorporates parity superselection and models noise using local depolarizing noise.

**Key observables.** Uhlmann-Wootters concurrences ($C_+(U, p)$ and $C_-(U, p)$) are used to diagnose the convex Gaussian nature of the noisy channel.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The noise probability $p$ is the key parameter, with the derived limit being $p = (8 - 2\sqrt{6})/5 \approx 62\%$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The bound is not directly comparable to previous work due to differences in the noise model applied to the gate set.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the noise model (gate followed by local depolarizing noise) and show numerical results plotting diagnostic quantities ($\Delta_{\pm}$ and commutator sums) against the noise parameter $p$.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem of noise thresholds, details the mathematical framework using fermionic Choi states and parity projections, derives the necessary concurrence formulas, and finally solves for the critical noise parameter $p$.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Determining the highest amount of noise that quantum circuits can handle is an interesting and crucial task in the development of fault-tolerant quantum computation. Previous work has constrained this upper limit for local depolarizing noise to $\approx 45~\%$ for circuits constructed using the universal Clifford with T gate set by finding the noise threshold where the gate set loses universality. In this work, we use a similar method with the matchgate with non-Gaussian resource universal gate set to find a limit of $p=(8 - 2 \sqrt{6})/5$ or $\approx 62~\%$ for fermionic quantum computing that is independent of circuit depth. To do this, we use Uhlmann-Wootters concurrences for a 4-mode fermionic Choi state representing a resourceful gate combined with local depolarizing noise to determine when the combined channel is convex Gaussian. These bounds are not directly comparable due to differences in noise model making the bound of $\approx 62~\%$ the best known for fermions.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper proves that the Holevo barycenter of a quantum channel is generally not multiplicative under the tensor product. By constructing specific channels, the authors show that the barycenter of the product channel does not equal the tensor product of the individual barycenters. This result deepens our understanding of quantum channel capacities by demonstrating that simple algebraic rules fail even when related concepts like capacity additivity are studied.

**Why it may be interesting.** The findings challenge simple tensor product assumptions in quantum information theory, suggesting that complex resource measures like the Holevo barycenter exhibit non-trivial, context-dependent behavior when composing channels.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the multiplicativity problem for the Holevo barycenter of quantum channels, asking if the barycenter of a product channel equals the tensor product of the individual barycenters.

**Main result.** The Holevo barycenter is proven to be non-multiplicative under the tensor product of the channel with itself, and the entropy of the barycenter is neither universally subadditive nor universally superadditive.

**Method.** The authors use theoretical derivations comparing block weights derived from the product channel ($\Omega(N \otimes N)$) against the tensor product of the individual barycenters ($\Omega(N) \otimes \Omega(N)$).

**Model / system.** The study concerns general quantum channels $N: L(H) 	o L(K)$ acting on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, often analyzed using direct-sum constructions ($N = N_0 \oplus N_1 \oplus N_2$).

**Key observables.** Holevo Capacity ($\chi(N)$), Holevo Barycenter ($\Omega(N)$), Von Neumann Entropy ($H(\cdot)$), and block weights derived from channel compositions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis depends on the structure of the channels, particularly comparing cases where $\chi(N_0) = \chi(N_1)$ versus $\chi(N_0) = \chi(N_1) + \delta$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** All Hilbert spaces are assumed to be finite-dimensional. The entropy comparisons rely on specific structural assumptions about the block states.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the context by relating Holevo capacity additivity to barycenter tensorization. It then constructs specific channels and uses entropy and block weight comparisons to prove the non-multiplicativity of the barycenter and the lack of universal entropic ordering.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Holevo barycenter of a quantum channel is the unique output state obtained as the average output of any ensemble achieving the Holevo capacity. Given two quantum channels, the multiplicativity problem asks whether this barycenter tensorizes under parallel composition, namely whether the barycenter of the product channel coincides with the tensor product of the individual barycenters. This question is closely related to the additivity problem for the Holevo capacity: additivity implies tensorization of the Holevo barycenter, while tensorization alone is not sufficient for additivity. Although a construction is known that demonstrates the existence of channels with non-additive Holevo capacity, their corresponding Holevo barycenters still tensorize, leaving open whether multiplicativity might ultimately hold universally. Here, we answer this question in the negative by exhibiting channels for which the Holevo barycenter is not multiplicative under the tensor product of the channel with itself. Moreover, we show that the entropy of the Holevo barycenter is neither universally subadditive nor universally superadditive under tensor product.

</details>

### [On the Limits of Quantum Multiparty Simultaneous Communication](http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10289v1)

**Authors:** Pedro Montealegre, Ivan Rapaport, Jorge Valenzuela  
**Type:** theory · **Category:** quantum information and computing · **PDF:** <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.10289v1>  
**Analysis basis:** full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

**Summary.** This work analyzes the communication complexity of a multiparty coordination problem, showing that while public randomness offers a significant advantage, unentangled quantum communication does not surpass the power of classical private randomness in the bounded-error regime. The research establishes an exponential separation based on the number of players, providing deep insights into the role of shared randomness versus quantum superposition.

**Why it may be interesting.** The findings provide fundamental limits on how quantum information can simulate classical coordination mechanisms, which has implications for quantum cryptography and distributed quantum computation protocols.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper establishes an exponential separation between the communication power of classical shared randomness (public coins) and unentangled quantum communication in a multiparty setting.

**Main result.** It shows that for the generalized Index Coordination problem, quantum communication without shared entanglement offers no asymptotic advantage over classical private randomness in the bounded-error regime, while public randomness provides a significant advantage.

**Method.** The authors employ techniques like the Parity Collapse method and information-pooling arguments, utilizing the Arithmetic Mean-Geometric Mean inequality to derive lower bounds on message size.

**Model / system.** The study uses the Simultaneous Message Passing (SMP) model generalized to $k$ players, comparing the resources of classical private randomness, classical public randomness, and unentangled quantum superposition.

**Key observables.** Maximum message length required by the players, measured in bits (public coins) or qubits (quantum communication).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of players ($k$), the input size ($n$), and the error parameter ($\epsilon$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The quantum protocols considered lack shared entanglement or public coins, and the results hold for fixed error parameters $\epsilon$.

**Figures summary.** Not specified in the notes, but the paper relies on summarizing bounds in a table (Table 1) comparing message lengths across different models.

**Paper structure.** The paper first generalizes the Index Coordination problem to $k$ parties. It then derives lower bounds for the unambiguous and bounded-error regimes using techniques like the RAC inequality and AM-GM inequality, culminating in the explicit separation results.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Simultaneous Message Passing (SMP) model provides a fundamental framework for comparing classical and quantum communication. For two players, Gavinsky et al. (STOC 2006) established a separation underlying the incomparability of shared randomness and quantum communication: \textsc{Index Coordination} needs $O(\log n)$ public-coin bits but $Ω(n^{1/3})$ bounded-error qubits.   In this work, we establish a multiparty exponential separation through $\operatorname{IC}_{k,n}$, a natural $k$-party generalization of \textsc{Index Coordination}. Public-coin protocols solve it unambiguously with maximum message length $O(\log n)$ bits. In contrast, quantum SMP protocols without shared entanglement or public coins require maximum message length $Ω(n^{1-1/k})$ qubits in the unambiguous regime and $Ω(n^{(k-1)/(k+1)})$ qubits in the bounded-error regime. A classical private-coin protocol matches the unambiguous bound, so quantum communication provides no asymptotic advantage over private randomness in this regime. For fixed error parameters, all constants are independent of $k$, establishing the exponential separation for every integer-valued function $k=k(n)\ge2$, without restricting its growth. Both quantum lower bounds become $Ω(n)$ when $k\ge c\log n$ for any fixed $c>0$, matching the full-input protocol and yielding tight linear complexity in both regimes.   Our results demonstrate that quantum superposition cannot efficiently simulate the coordination afforded by public randomness, extending this separation to arbitrary $k$. To bound success probabilities for multiparty product states, we prove an exact factorization theorem for unambiguous quantum state identification, which may be of independent mathematical interest.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper tackles the superactivation problem in quantum information theory by demonstrating that two quantum channels, each having zero private capacity, can jointly support private communication. The authors achieve this by constructing a specific joint channel that yields a positive secure rate. This result proves that secure communication capacity cannot be determined by analyzing the private capacity of the individual channels in isolation.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a deep theoretical result showing that local capacity measures are insufficient for characterizing secure quantum communication, which is a fundamental question in quantum information theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper resolves the 'private-capacity superactivation' problem: determining if two quantum channels, each with zero individual private capacity, can jointly enable private communication.

**Main result.** The joint use of a four-level channel and a qubit erasure channel, both having zero private capacity, was shown to achieve a positive private rate, demonstrating that channel private capacity alone is insufficient to determine secure communication capability.

**Method.** The analysis involves constructing specific quantum channels and applying information-theoretic bounds, utilizing concepts like Holevo information and classical coding over multiple uses to establish a positive lower bound on the achievable private rate.

**Model / system.** The model uses two independent, memoryless quantum channels: a four-level channel and a qubit erasure channel. The analysis is highly abstract, relying on mathematical constructions and formal proofs in Lean 4.

**Key observables.** Private bits per product use, Holevo information ($\chi$), and the achievable rate $P(E_{2,p} \otimes N)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Erasure probability $p$ (specifically $p=1/2$), and the positive rate exceeding $1.9030 	imes 10^{-4}$ bits.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The proof relies on bounding the environment's leakage using a 'Classical coin bound' and assumes the applicability of the private coding theorem.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 summarizes the logical dependencies of the formalized argument, while Table 1 provides a detailed correspondence between paper statements and their Lean declarations.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the problem by first establishing the necessary information-theoretic bounds (using Holevo information and entropy curvature) and then constructing a concrete example (the joint channel use) to achieve a positive rate, culminating in a formalization within the Lean proof assistant.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Private communication over a noisy quantum channel requires reliable transmission to the receiver and secrecy from the environment. Whether two channels with zero private capacity can jointly enable private communication is a longstanding open problem in quantum information theory. Here we resolve this problem by exhibiting a four-level channel and a qubit erasure channel with half erasure probability, each with zero private capacity, whose joint use achieves more than 0.0001903 private bits per product use. The encoding gives the receiver a linear information gain with at most quadratic environmental leakage, enabling privacy through a fixed joint measurement and classical coding. This superactivation, impossible for independent classical memoryless wiretap channels, shows that a channel's private capacity alone does not determine its value for secure communication. The initial activation example was identified through interactions with large language models, and the result has been formalized in Lean 4.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes the conditions for the spread of costly cooperation on weighted networks by modeling a donation game. It derives sharp mathematical thresholds for the benefit-to-cost ratio required for cooperation to invade. The methodology uses advanced techniques from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics to quantify the structural requirements for collective traits to persist against natural selection.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous mathematical framework for analyzing the emergence of cooperation via selection thresholds on complex networks connects concepts from statistical physics (non-equilibrium dynamics, critical phenomena) to evolutionary game theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the conditions under which costly cooperation can spread and persist within a population structured on a weighted network.

**Main result.** It determines sharp weak-selection thresholds for cooperation, finding specific ratios of benefit to cost ($b/c$) required for fixation on different network structures like cycles and paths.

**Method.** The analysis employs techniques from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, including fluctuation response, first-passage time calculations, and optimization over network weights.

**Model / system.** The model is a donation game played on a finite, weighted, undirected graph where traits (cooperator/defector) are inherited via copying based on weighted contacts.

**Key observables.** Weak-selection threshold ($b/c$), fixation advantage ($\Delta$), and the minimal contact contrast required for a given threshold.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The selection strength ($\epsilon$), the benefit ($b$), the cost ($c$), and the network topology (e.g., $C_4, P_5, P_6$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is restricted to the source-first, averaged-payoff process, and comparisons are made between individual payoff dominance and population-level fixation advantage.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate small supports, showing the minimal promoter structures for cooperation on a four-cycle ($C_4$), five-site path ($P_5$), and six-site path ($P_6$).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the game and dynamics on weighted networks, to calculating fixation probabilities and susceptibility, and finally performing rigorous optimization to find the minimal structural requirements for sustained cooperation.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

A costly inherited trait can spread when its descendants create a favorable local environment. We ask which finite contact structures sustain such a collective competitor and what their advantage costs. Individuals play a donation game, conferring benefit $b$ at cost $c$. Reciprocal weighted contacts determine averaged payoffs and copying recipients, while sources are chosen globally according to payoff. Cooperation is favored when a uniformly introduced cooperator takes over more often than a defector in the complementary experiment. Exact fluctuation response and elimination of fast configurations identify the formation and competition of protected domains as the controlling processes. The sharp weak-selection threshold infima are $b/c=3$ on the four-cycle, $7$ on the five-site path, and $1$ on every fixed path with at least six sites. On the six-site path, a global bound forces near-barrier designs into this domain hierarchy. Polynomial relations among the contact ratios then control unrestricted optimization and imply eventual exact reflection symmetry. Reaching threshold $1+ε$ requires minimum contact contrast $656ε^{-2}[1+O(ε)]$ and neutral absorption time of order $ε^{-1}$. We determine their tradeoff and the associated design tolerance. Finite selection consumes the same margin. Within the controlled small-selection window, the maximal fixation advantage is of order $ε^{5/2}$ when the contrast exceeds its exact minimum by order $ε^{-1}$. Thus an improving invasion threshold can require increasing contact heterogeneity, precision and observation time.

</details>

**Summary.** This work tests if quantum feature engineering, implemented via an IQP circuit, can boost credit default prediction accuracy beyond what is achievable with classical feature extraction methods like Kernel PCA. By appending 16 quantum features to a Logistic Regression model, the authors achieved a statistically significant performance gain, suggesting that quantum circuits can effectively map classical data into a richer feature space beneficial for linear classifiers.

**Why it may be interesting.** It explores the practical application of quantum feature mapping in a real-world, high-stakes classification problem, providing quantitative evidence for the potential utility of quantum circuits in enhancing classical machine learning models.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates whether quantum feature engineering using Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time (IQP) circuits can provide a statistically significant advantage in improving a linear classifier for credit default prediction over classical methods.

**Main result.** Appending 16 IQP features to a Logistic Regression model raised the F1 score by +0.055, significantly outperforming Kernel PCA (0.493) and the raw baseline (0.462), with the advantage surviving rigorous statistical correction.

**Method.** The authors encode classical financial features into rotation angles ($	heta_i$) and use an $n$-qubit IQP circuit (Hadamard $ightarrow R_Z ightarrow ZZ$ ring) to generate $2n$ expectation values as quantum features, which are then used in a Logistic Regression model.

**Model / system.** The model is an $n$-qubit IQP circuit, which runs in constant depth and encodes feature correlations in a $2^n$-dimensional Hilbert space. The quantum features are appended to the original classical features for classification.

**Key observables.** F1 score, Accuracy, AUC, and the expectation values $\langle X_i angle$ and $\langle Y_i angle$ for each qubit.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Number of qubits ($n=8$), number of features (16 quantum features), and the feature budget constraint used for comparison.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The quantum advantage is demonstrated on a classical simulator, and the comparison is specifically limited to improving a linear classifier, suggesting a mechanism of external non-linearity injection.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the 8-qubit IQP feature extractor sequence: Hadamard superposition $ightarrow R_Z$ data-encoding $ightarrow ZZ$ ring entanglement, followed by X and Y basis measurements.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem (credit risk), details the quantum feature construction (IQP circuit), compares the resulting features against classical benchmarks (KPCA, linear transformations) using rigorous statistical testing (BH correction), and analyzes the mechanism of improvement (linearity).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Credit default prediction is a tabular classification problem in which modest gains in F1 translate directly into reduced financial exposure. We ask whether Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time (IQP) circuits can produce features that improve a classifier over both its raw classical baseline and Kernel PCA - the strongest unsupervised classical non-linear alternative - at an equal feature budget. The dataset provides 23 financial attributes per client; for an n-qubit circuit we select n of them, encode each as a rotation angle, and read 2n expectation values back out as new features. The motivation for using a quantum circuit is computational: an n-qubit IQP circuit runs in constant depth and encodes feature correlations in a 2^n-dimensional Hilbert space, whereas classical simulation of its exact output statistics scales exponentially in n. Using the UCI Default of Credit Card Clients dataset and five-fold cross-validation, we find that appending 16 IQP features (n = 8 qubits) to a Logistic Regression model raises F1 from 0.462 to 0.517 (+0.055, p < 0.0001). Kernel PCA, the next-best method, reaches only 0.493 at the same feature count; the gap survives Benjamini-Hochberg correction across 12 tests (p = 0.00007). No other classifier - Random Forest, SVM, XGBoost, or k-NN - benefits, which points to a linear-expressivity mechanism rather than a generic improvement. We also show that how the 8 input features are chosen matters: Random Forest importance-guided selection reaches F1 = 0.523, while encoding maximally uncorrelated features drops it to 0.496, demonstrating that the circuit amplifies informative structure rather than creating it from scratch.

</details>

**Summary.** This work uses Diffusion Monte Carlo simulations to calculate the static response functions of the 3D electron gas in the strongly coupled regime. The authors identify a distinct structural feature in the local field factor G(q) at intermediate wave vectors. This feature is argued to be a direct signature of short-range order, providing a crucial benchmark for understanding electronic correlations beyond simple approximations.

**Why it may be interesting.** The study provides benchmark data on electronic correlations in a fundamental model, which is crucial for developing accurate theoretical inputs for many-body calculations relevant to correlated materials.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to accurately determine the wave-vector-dependent static local field factor G(q) and the static density-density response function for the 3D electron gas, particularly in the strongly coupled (low-density) regime.

**Main result.** The calculations reveal a pronounced, non-trivial structure in G(q) at intermediate wave vectors, which is identified as a fingerprint of short-range order and is necessary to correctly reproduce the static structure factor.

**Method.** The primary method involves using Diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) simulations to calculate the response functions, which are then analyzed using theoretical parametrizations.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is the three-dimensional electron gas (HEG), a fundamental model in condensed matter physics used as a starting point for ab initio calculations of materials.

**Key observables.** Static local field factor G(q), static density-density response function $\chi(q)$, and the static structure factor $S(q)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The Wigner-Seitz radius ($r_s$), which controls the coupling strength, is varied across the strongly coupled regime ($r_s > 10$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on DMC calculations for benchmark data and utilizes the Single-Mode Approximation (SMA) for certain derived quantities.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate G(q) vs $r_s$ showing the structural feature, the exchange-correlation kernel $f_{	ext{xc}}(r)$ confirming real-space structure, and $\chi(q)$ and $S(q)$ showing the correlated structure.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical problem, presents DMC calculations of $\chi(q)$ and $G(q)$ across various densities, identifies the structural feature in $G(q)$ required by $S(q)$, and discusses the implications for low-energy resonant modes.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The three-dimensional electron gas is a fundamental model in condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry, and the exchange-correlation energy derived from it serves as the starting point of \textit{ab initio} computations of materials. However, the wave-vector-dependent response, and hence the static local field factor $G(q)$, has remained without accurate ground-state benchmark in the strongly coupled regime for three decades. Using diffusion Monte Carlo, we calculate $G(q)$ and the static density-density response function across the liquid phase and find a pronounced structure in $G(q)$ at intermediate wave vectors, already visible at metallic densities and growing with increasing interaction strength. We identify it as a fingerprint of short-range order by showing that it is required to reproduce the static structure factor. Our parametrization, valid in the entire liquid phase, predicts a low-energy resonant mode inside the particle-hole continuum.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a novel, computationally efficient method to calculate certified lower bounds on the keyrates for QKD protocols like BB84. By reformulating complex optimization problems using tangent-line approximations, the authors make these calculations tractable for standard convex solvers. This advances the theoretical understanding of achievable secure key rates in quantum cryptography.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous mathematical techniques developed for bounding keyrates using convex optimization and tangent lines provide powerful, generalizable tools for analyzing information-theoretic security in quantum communication.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the computation of finite-size keyrates for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols, aiming to provide certified lower bounds.

**Main result.** The authors propose using tangent-line approximations to transform complex, non-convex optimization problems into computationally tractable convex forms, yielding certified lower bounds for the keyrate.

**Method.** The core method involves reformulating the keyrate optimization problem to utilize convex optimization solvers by deriving suitable tangent lines to the lower bound terms in the objective function.

**Model / system.** The analysis focuses on QKD protocols, specifically the qubit BB84 and the six-state protocol, often modeled using entanglement-based forms and Werner states.

**Key observables.** Finite-size keyrate ($\ell_{	ext{key}}$), Rényi entropy ($	ext{H}^{\uparrow}_{\alpha}, 	ext{H}^{\downarrow}_{\alpha}$), and the asymptotic keyrate ($	ext{r}_{	ext{asymp}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Rényi entropy parameter ($\alpha$), security parameter ($\varepsilon_{	ext{secure}}$), and test-round probability ($\gamma$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The keyrate bound is derived using a tangent-line lower bound approximation, meaning the computed rate is guaranteed to be less than or equal to the true achievable rate.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the convergence of the computed keyrate as the number of tangent lines or the grid size increases, showing the rate plateaus at sufficient computational effort.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the general problem of keyrate computation via convex optimization, then details the tangent-line approximation technique for simple protocols like BB84, and finally extends this to derive closed-form entropy expressions for the six-state protocol.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Recent work in quantum key distribution (QKD) has yielded finite-size keyrates based on convex optimisation problems, using the framework of entropy accumulation. Multiple solvers have been developed to address these optimisations in recent years, but have been based on a somewhat elaborate framework using sophisticated algorithms, in order to accommodate a broad range of QKD protocols. In this work, we note that for basic QKD protocols such as qubit BB84, the keyrates can be easily computed using off-the-shelf solvers instead, by obtaining suitable tangent lines to lower bound terms in the objective function. We compute the resulting finite-size keyrates and compare them to previous work. Moreover, we extend this approach to the six-state protocol, by deriving closed-form expressions for the single-round Rényi entropies in the protocol. This should facilitate subsequent study of the six-state protocol via entropy accumulation.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper derives tight, fine-grained lower bounds for the quantum query complexity of distinguishing between two Hamming weights using the Multiplicative Adversary Method. By relating this problem to the unique OR problem, the authors establish a complex lower bound that precisely characterizes the required number of quantum queries in the small-bias regime.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous application of the multiplicative adversary method to derive fine-grained lower bounds provides a powerful, query-by-query understanding of quantum distinguishability, which is relevant for understanding resource scaling in quantum algorithms.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper studies the quantum query complexity required to distinguish between two specific Hamming weights, $|x|=M$ versus $|x|=M+\Delta$, in the small-bias regime.

**Main result.** It establishes a fine-grained lower bound for this quantum counting problem, showing the complexity scales with a maximum of two terms derived from the multiplicative adversary method.

**Method.** The primary technique is the Multiplicative Adversary Method (MADV), which is applied to analyze the progress of quantum distinguishability across different Hamming-weight layers.

**Model / system.** The model is a quantum query algorithm operating on an input space $\{0,1\}^N$, where the goal is to distinguish between two subsets defined by their Hamming weights. The analysis uses concepts from the eigenspace method for symmetric functions.

**Key observables.** The success probability margin $\zeta$, and the quantum query complexity $Q$ (or $T$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Total bits $N$, the two weights $M$ and $M+\Delta$, and the bias parameter $\zeta$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the success probability is at least $1/2 + \zeta$, and often assumes $M+\Delta \le N-M$ for the primary derivation.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds the lower bound by first analyzing the unique OR problem using MADV, then reducing this to the two-weight counting problem, and finally combining these results to yield the overall complexity bound.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the two-weight decision version of quantum approximate counting: given oracle access to $x\in\{0,1\}^N$, distinguish $|x|=M$ from $|x|=M+Δ$ with success probability $1/2+ζ$. Using the multiplicative adversary method, we prove $Ω\left(\max\left\{ζ\sqrt{(N-M)(M+Δ)}/Δ,\sqrt{ζN/Δ}\right\}\right)$. The same parameter dependence follows from the polynomial-method characterization of the two-layer symmetric function by Podder, Yao, and Ye. Our contribution is a multiplicative-adversary derivation that tracks the progress produced by individual oracle queries. For the first term, after complementing the input if necessary, we assume $M+Δ\le N-M$. We use the Hamming-layer subspaces from the eigenspace method of Ambainis, Spalek, and de Wolf and compose their adjacent-layer unitary maps to relate the two nonadjacent promise layers. After fixing the queried coordinate, the analysis block-diagonalizes into four-dimensional subspaces. An exact calculation of the one-query progress ratio gives the first lower bound. The same estimate also implies $\left\|(I-\widehatΠ_{\mathrm{bad}})\lvertΨ^T\rangle\right\|^2=O\left(T^2Δ^2/((N-M)(M+Δ))\right)$ for the coherent input superposition used in the adversary argument. For the second term, we prove directly using a three-eigenvalue multiplicative adversary that unique OR on $n$ bits with success probability $1/2+ζ$ requires $Ω(\sqrt{ζn})$ queries, and then reduce unique OR to the two-weight counting problem.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a quantum algorithm to solve wave propagation PDEs by reformulating the problem as geometric quantum state preparation. It overcomes the exponential inefficiency of standard Fourier-space methods, which fail due to singularities on the resonant manifold. The resulting technique allows for efficient computation whose success probability scales favorably with the number of sources but remains independent of the system size.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete quantum algorithmic approach to solving fundamental physics problems (wave propagation) where standard quantum simulation techniques fail due to inherent mathematical singularities, offering a path toward practical quantum simulation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of using quantum algorithms to solve wave propagation partial differential equations (PDEs), particularly the Helmholtz equation, which suffer from singularities in the frequency domain.

**Main result.** The authors propose a novel method that bypasses the exponential overhead of standard Fourier-space solvers by directly preparing quantum states supported on the resonant manifold, yielding a success probability independent of the domain size.

**Method.** The core method involves recasting the PDE solution as a geometric quantum state preparation problem, utilizing quantum circuits to construct superpositions over the resonant manifold rather than inverting the full discretized operator.

**Model / system.** The model is wave propagation governed by PDEs like the Helmholtz equation. The problem is discretized and analyzed in the frequency domain, leading to a linear system whose inverse is singular on the dispersion surface $k^2 = \omega^2/c^2$.

**Key observables.** Success probability of state preparation ($P_{	ext{res}}$), which is shown to be independent of the computational domain size.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The condition number of the discretized operator ($\kappa(A)$), the resonant manifold ($k^2 = \omega^2/c^2$), and the number of sources.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method relies on approximating the inverse operator structure and assumes the ability to perform complex arithmetic evaluation and post-selection on amplitude coefficients.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the quantum circuits for preparing a resonant state, including implementing a quantum analogue of the Midpoint circle algorithm and extending this to construct a finite-width resonant ring.

**Paper structure.** The paper first contrasts standard Quantum Linear System Solvers (QLSS) with the limitations imposed by the condition number. It then details the failure of direct Fourier-space methods due to singularities, culminating in the proposal and derivation of the geometric quantum state preparation technique.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present a quantum algorithm for solving partial differential equations through a linear-system formulation, focusing on wave propagation problems described by the discretized Helmholtz equation in frequency domain. Although quantum linear-system solvers offer exponential compression of the system degrees of freedom, their runtime complexity is generally governed by the condition number of the discretized operator. Exploiting the analytic structure of the differential operator can provide an alternative to explicit matrix inversion, as illustrated for the screened Poisson equation through an explicit quantum circuit. For the Helmholtz equation, however, the inverse operator becomes singular on the dispersion surface $k^2=ω^2/c^2$, rendering direct Fourier-space state-preparation methods exponentially inefficient. We address this challenge by directly preparing quantum states supported on the resonant manifold and encoding source locations through Fourier phases. The resulting algorithm eliminates the exponentially large overhead associated with post-selection on the resonant manifold, yielding a success probability that depends linearly on the number of sources and is independent of the computational domain size. More generally, our approach applies to hyperbolic differential equations whose Fourier-space solutions possess singular support on dispersion manifolds, recasting their solution as a problem of geometric quantum state preparation.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical study investigates how altermagnetism, characterized by a specific magnetic anisotropy ($\delta J_2$), alters the two-magnon light scattering spectrum. The authors demonstrate that this anisotropy causes a distinct, momentum-dependent shift in the two-magnon continuum edges and lifts degeneracies in the resonance peaks. These findings establish a powerful spectroscopic tool for identifying altermagnetic order in insulating magnets.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides a concrete, measurable spectroscopic signature (momentum-dependent two-magnon shift) that can be sought using advanced techniques like RIXS to distinguish altermagnets from other magnetic phases.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is identifying the unique spectroscopic fingerprints of altermagnetism, particularly through multi-magnon excitations.

**Main result.** The altermagnetic exchange anisotropy ($\delta J_2$) causes a measurable, momentum-dependent shift in the upper edge of the two-magnon continuum and lifts degeneracies in the two-magnon resonance.

**Method.** The study uses linear spin-wave theory supplemented by leading 1/S quantum corrections and calculates the two-magnon light scattering intensity.

**Model / system.** The system is a two-dimensional d-wave altermagnet modeled by an effective Heisenberg Hamiltonian on a Lieb lattice, characterized by the anisotropy parameter $\delta J_2 = J_{2a} - J_{2b}$.

**Key observables.** Two-magnon light scattering intensity, the energy shift of the upper continuum edge at $\mathbf{X}=(\pi,0)$, and the splitting of the two-magnon resonance at $\mathbf{K}=(\pi/2,\pi/2)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The anisotropy parameter $|\delta J_2|$ dictates the magnitude of the spectral shifts, which are found to be linear in $|\delta J_2|$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The calculations rely on linear spin-wave theory extended with leading $1/S$ quantum corrections and treating magnon-magnon interactions within the ladder approximation.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the Lieb lattice structure and the momentum-dependent shifts in the two-magnon continuum edges and resonance splitting as a function of $\delta J_2$.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using spin-wave theory to calculate the two-magnon scattering intensity. It then presents quantitative results showing the momentum-selective shifts caused by $\delta J_2$ compared to conventional antiferromagnets, followed by detailed analysis of the resonance splitting.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Altermagnetism is a recently established class of magnetic order that combines fully compensated moments with momentum-dependent spin splitting, yet identifying its spectroscopic fingerprints remains an open challenge. In this work, we investigate finite-momentum two-magnon excitations in a two-dimensional $d$-wave altermagnet by calculating the two-magnon light scattering intensity in different polarization channels. Using linear spin-wave theory and further incorporating the leading $1/S$ quantum corrections, we demonstrate that the characteristic magnon splitting of altermagnets shifts the upper edge of the two-magnon continuum and the corresponding spectral features to higher energy at $\boldsymbol{X}=(π,0)$ relative to the conventional antiferromagnet, by an amount linear in the exchange anisotropy $|δJ_2|$, while leaving the response at the Brillouin-zone center unchanged. Although magnon-magnon interactions strongly redistribute spectral weight toward lower energies, the energy scale associated with the high-energy momentum-selective reconstruction remains robust. The interactions additionally generate a pronounced low-energy two-peak structure that has no counterpart within linear spin-wave theory. At $\boldsymbol{K}=(π/2,π/2)$, we show that the interacting two-magnon resonance is twofold degenerate in the conventional antiferromagnetic phase, while a finite altermagnetic exchange anisotropy lifts this degeneracy, producing two peaks whose separation is linear in $|δJ_2|$. The characteristic energy scales underlying both features are intrinsic to the two-magnon sector rather than to a specific scattering operator. These findings highlight the potential of finite-momentum two-magnon spectroscopy for identifying altermagnetic order in insulating magnets and motivate momentum-resolved resonant inelastic x-ray scattering studies of candidate altermagnetic materials.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper determines the locations where the entangling power of a unitary quantum gate reaches an extremum. It proves that these stationary points occur at specific 'corner' configurations defined by the relative eigenphases of the unitary. This work provides a powerful tool for classifying quantum gates based on their entanglement properties.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a rigorous mathematical characterization of when and where entanglement generation is extremal for quantum gates, linking fundamental algebraic properties ($U^2 \propto \mathbb{I}$) to physical observables.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the stationary points of the entangling power generated by a unitary operator acting on a bipartite Hilbert space.

**Main result.** The entangling power is proven to be stationary at specific 'corner' points in the relative eigenphase torus, where the unitary takes the form of a generalized reflection $R = \mathbb{I} - 2Q$.

**Method.** The analysis uses the spectral decomposition of the unitary operator and calculates the entangling power as a function of relative eigenphases, identifying critical points via differentiation.

**Model / system.** The system is a bipartite Hilbert space acted upon by a finite-dimensional unitary operator $U$. The analysis is illustrated using two-qubit gates and two-site spin chains.

**Key observables.** Entangling power ($E_p$), which is defined using the average linear entropy $\langle E(|\psiangle) angle$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The relative eigenphases ($\delta_a$) of the unitary operator, and the invariants ($\alpha, eta$) derived from the spectral projectors.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the unitary can be parameterized by relative eigenphases, and the theorem only locates stationary points, not classifying them fully.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the entangling power $E_p$ near stationary corners for specific physical models, such as the two-site spin-1 BLBQ Hamiltonian, showing how the extremum type depends on the trajectory.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the general mathematical framework by analyzing the dependence of $E_p$ on relative phases, proves the existence of stationary points at the corners, derives the form of the corner unitaries ($R_m$), and then applies these results to concrete physical examples like two-qubit gates and spin chains.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The entangling power of a unitary operator acting on a bipartite Hilbert space measures the entanglement it generates from product states, averaged over the inputs. A finite-dimensional unitary has a spectral decomposition $U=\sum_{a=1}^{n}e^{iθ_a}P_a$, where $e^{iθ_a}$ are the eigenvalues, $P_a$ the corresponding eigen-projectors, and $n$ is the number of distinct eigenvalues. After removing an overall phase, the entangling power is a function on the $(n-1)$-torus of relative eigenphases at fixed spectral projectors. We prove that this function is stationary at all $2^{n-1}$ points on the torus where every relative phase is $0$ or $π$, which we define as \textit{corners}. Up to an overall phase, $U$ at each corner is a generalized reflection $R=\mathbb{I}-2Q$ satisfying $R^2=\mathbb{I}$, where $Q$ is the sum of spectral projectors whose relative phase is $π$. At the corner the entangling power is expressed in terms of seven local-unitary invariants of $Q$. A unitary gate $U$ can be realized as a corner of some projector family if and only if $U^2\propto\mathbb{I}$, a condition satisfied by many Clifford and non-Clifford gates. We illustrate the theorem with two-qubit gates, $SU(N)$ channel decompositions, and two-site spin chains, obtaining examples of minima, maxima, and saddle points. In addition, a corner that is a saddle point on the full phase torus can appear as a local maximum or minimum along different time-evolution trajectories.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces the synergetic method, a novel numerical technique designed to overcome the computational stiffness encountered when simulating systems with widely separated timescales. By projecting the dynamics onto the slowly evolving modes, the method efficiently models the long-term interaction and pattern formation of solitons in optical resonators, enabling simulations on realistic laboratory timescales.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work presents a powerful, generalizable numerical technique for analyzing complex, slow dynamics in nonlinear physical systems, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems and nonlinear wave physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is numerically simulating the slow, long-term evolution of complex soliton patterns in optical resonators, where the dynamics are governed by timescales vastly different from the rapid damping timescales.

**Main result.** The authors developed and applied the 'synergetic method' to simulate multi-soliton interactions, achieving speedups of $10^3$ to $10^5$ times over conventional methods and modeling dynamics on laboratory timescales.

**Method.** The synergetic method, inspired by Haken's framework, eliminates rapidly damped degrees-of-freedom by analyzing the Jacobian of the evolution equation, projecting the dynamics onto the slow, dominant eigenmodes.

**Model / system.** The system is based on dissipative Kerr solitons in a driven nonlinear Kerr cavity, modeled by the Lugiato-Lefever equation (a driven-damped nonlinear Schrödinger equation).

**Key observables.** Inter-soliton separations ($p_1, p_2$), the potential function $U(p_1, p_2)$, and the dynamical spectrum (eigenvalues) of the linearized operator.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The separation between fast (damping) and slow (pattern evolution) timescales, and the ability to simulate dynamics over laboratory timescales (e.g., seconds).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method assumes that the long-term behavior is governed by a small cluster of eigenvalues near zero, corresponding to the slow collective dynamics.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the system's dynamics, showing the evolution of soliton patterns (single, molecule, crystal) and mapping the potential energy landscape $U(p_1, p_2)$ that governs the slow convergence of the system.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical context (solitons in microresonators), identifies the computational bottleneck (stiffness due to timescale separation), proposes the synergetic method based on Jacobian analysis, and validates it by simulating complex multi-soliton interactions and mapping their potential energy surfaces.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Complex patterns in physical and biological systems often emerge through slow collective dynamics governed by a small number of key variables. In nonlinear optical resonators, dissipative Kerr solitons provide an important example, where interactions between well-separated solitons can evolve over timescales far longer than the characteristic loss and gain timescales. Direct numerical simulation of these dynamics is challenging because stiffness forces conventional methods to resolve many rapidly damped degrees-of-freedom with very small time steps. We present a numerical scheme, the synergetic method, that eliminates these rapidly damped degrees-of-freedom and retains the slowly evolving modes, enabling time steps many orders of magnitude larger than those used in conventional approaches. Applied to soliton molecules in driven Kerr cavities, the method achieves speedups of $10^3$ to $10^5$ while capturing dynamics on laboratory timescales. We use it to model the full interaction dynamics of a three-soliton molecule and the evolution of an eight-soliton molecule. The approach provides an efficient framework for studying slow pattern formation in nonlinear systems with widely separated timescales.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces the MIDAS method for self-assembling gold nanocubes on surfaces, achieving high control over the resulting 2D or 3D superstructures. The assembly mechanism is governed by depletion forces interacting with the substrate's surface morphology. This establishes a generalizable framework for fabricating ordered nanoparticle arrays for plasmonic applications.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical colloidal assembly, the underlying principles of controlled self-organization, phase transitions driven by external fields (depletion potential), and the use of computational models (KMC, lattice-gas) are highly relevant to understanding many-body dynamics in quantum systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is achieving precise, controllable, and scalable large-scale self-assembly of nanoparticles into functional structures, overcoming limitations in current methods.

**Main result.** The MIDAS method successfully enables the facile, selective formation of 2D and 3D nanoparticle arrays whose structure is dictated by the interplay between depletion forces and substrate surface roughness.

**Method.** The study combines experimental assembly using gold nanocubes (AuNCs) with theoretical modeling, including lattice-gas modeling and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations.

**Model / system.** The system involves AuNCs assembling on various substrates (Si, glass) driven by depletion forces generated by a depletant (BDAC micelles). The assembly mode (2D vs 3D) is controlled by the substrate's surface roughness and interaction strength.

**Key observables.** 2D and 3D assembled monolayers/multilayers (AuNAMs), lattice constants, interparticle gaps, and UV-Vis reflectance spectra.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Substrate surface roughness ($	ext{Sa}$), depletion potential ($U_{dep}$), and the relative strength of nanoparticle-substrate vs. nanoparticle-nanoparticle interactions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The growth mode is determined by comparing the attractive nanoparticle-substrate interactions against the nanoparticle-nanoparticle interactions, which is further refined by surface roughness control.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the assembly process (dropcasting) and the resulting structures, showing 2D AuNAMs on smooth Si and 3D AuNAMs on less smooth glass.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the MIDAS method, details the role of depletion forces and substrate properties in determining the growth regime (2D vs 3D), and validates these findings using both in situ microscopy and computational modeling.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Self-assembling nanoparticles is a highly efficient and facile way to form functional nano-, micro- and macrostructures. However, currently available methods lack precision and controllability in size, shape and composition, suffer from poor reproducibility and scalability, and require complex steps and expensive materials. Here, we present the uniform morphology-induced and depletion force-directed nanoparticle assembly on surface (MIDAS) method with gold nanocubes (AuNCs). Using this approach, morphology-sensitive depletion forces trigger shape-selective flocculation and assembly of the AuNCs with uniform size and shape. Importantly, the surface roughness-controlled substrate drives the large-scale formation of AuNC-assembled monolayers (2D AuNAMs) or three-dimensional AuNC-assembled multilayers (3D AuNAMs) in a highly specific manner without any complex ligand modification or preparation steps. Lattice-gas modeling and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations show the depletion force is the key parameter determining supercrystal morphology and corroborate the experimental findings. This work establishes a generalizable nanoparticle assembly mechanism and demonstrates the broad applicability of the MIDAS strategy for scalable fabrication and patterning of 2D and 3D nanoparticle architectures.

</details>

**Summary.** This work reports on the quantum phase transitions in rhombohedral graphene moiré superlattices, identifying the Fractional Quantized Anomalous Hall Insulator (FQAHI) phase. By analyzing transport measurements, the authors show that phase boundaries follow predictable semi-circle relations, and by fitting temperature dependence, they estimate the energy gaps in these exotic correlated insulating states.

**Why it may be interesting.** The study provides experimental evidence for highly correlated insulating states (FCIs/FQAHI) in a tunable 2D platform, which is crucial for understanding topological phases relevant to quantum simulation and emergent quantum phenomena.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates quantum phase transitions and characterizes novel insulating states, specifically the Fractional Quantized Anomalous Hall Insulator (FQAHI), in rhombohedral graphene moiré superlattices.

**Main result.** Phase transitions between various correlated states (FL, FCI, CI) are described by semi-circle relations in resistivity/conductivity space, confirming the existence of a new FQAHI phase.

**Method.** The study combines systematic transport measurements (resistivity/conductivity) with theoretical modeling, employing the effective medium approximation and fitting temperature-dependent data to thermal activation models.

**Model / system.** The physical system is rhombohedral pentalayer graphene/hBN moiré superlattices, which exhibit tunable electronic properties via an external gate-displacement field (D). The analysis covers transitions between Composite Fermi liquid, Fermi liquid, and Fractional Chern Insulator states.

**Key observables.** Longitudinal and transverse resistivities/conductivities ($ho_{xx}, ho_{xy}$), which exhibit semi-circle trajectories; temperature-dependent resistance ($R_{xx}$); and estimated transport gap sizes.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Gate-displacement field ($D$), filling factor ($
u$), and temperature ($T$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The semi-circle law is assumed to hold for two-phase coexistence, and the analysis relies on fitting data to specific functional forms (e.g., thermal activation or $T^2$ dependence).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate semi-circle transitions in $(ho_{xx}, ho_{xy})$ and $(\sigma_{xx}, \sigma_{xy})$ planes for different filling factors, alongside Arrhenius plots comparing thermal activation fits to metallic temperature dependencies.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes transport measurements across different filling factors, first establishing the semi-circle law for phase transitions, then detailing the FCI-CI transition suggesting the FQAHI, and finally using temperature-dependent fits to estimate transport gaps.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect (FQAHE) has been discovered in twisted MoTe$_2$ and rhombohedral graphene/hBN moiré superlattices. Such van der Waals heterostructures feature a tuning knob of gate displacement field $D$, which is absent from the conventional fractional quantum Hall systems in two-dimensional electron gases. $D$ plays a critical role in engineering FQAHE and other emergent quantum states and provides an exciting new opportunity to explore their quantum phase transitions. However, the microscopic details of such transitions and temperature-dependent transport have remained mostly elusive. Here we report systematic resistance measurements in rhombohedral pentalayer graphene/hBN moiré superlattices. We found that the displacement field-driven phase transitions between Composite Fermi liquid, Fermi liquid, Fractional Chern insulators, and insulating states are described by semi-circle relations of the longitudinal and transverse resistivities (or conductivities), largely unexplored in the fractional quantum Hall systems. This agrees with a spatially separated two-phase picture for the phase transitions and further indicates a new insulator phase--fractional quantized anomalous Hall insulator. By comparing the temperature-dependence of longitudinal resistance with the thermal activation model, we estimated the transport gap sizes in three fractional Chern insulator states. Our work shed light on the quantum and temperature evolutions of fractional Chern insulator states--providing necessary background for anyon-braiding and gate-defined junctions in rhombohedral graphene.

</details>

**Summary.** This work demonstrates that near-field imaging of spin waves does not provide a direct map of the material's eigenmodes. By analyzing the interference between different spin-wave components, the authors show that apparent zero-momentum signals are artifacts of magnon-magnon interference, providing a necessary framework for interpreting complex wave measurements in magnonics.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of interpreting measured fields as interferometric spectra rather than intrinsic mode spectra is crucial for understanding wave phenomena in nanoscale devices, which has parallels in quantum optics and condensed matter wave physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The standard interpretation that spatially resolved measurements of coherent waves directly map the underlying eigenmode spectrum fails in near-field imaging of multimode spin-wave transport.

**Main result.** The observed low-momentum signals are not due to true propagating modes but arise from coherent magnon-magnon interference between directly excited and scattered spin waves.

**Method.** The study combines scanning nitrogen-vacancy (NV) magnetometry experiments with advanced theoretical modeling, including the Near-Field Diffraction (NFD) framework and Biot-Savart law calculations.

**Model / system.** The system is spin-wave transport in a yttrium iron garnet (YIG) film, probed by a local, phase-coherent microwave-field sensor (NV magnetometry). The signal is modeled as the superposition of multiple interfering magnetic fields.

**Key observables.** The measured signal's spatial Fourier components, particularly the anomalous components appearing near zero wave vector ($\mathbf{k} \approx 0$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Probe-sample distance ($d$), excitation wave vectors ($\mathbf{k}_{	ext{exc}}$) and scattering wave vectors ($\mathbf{k}_{	ext{scat}}$), and the difference wave vector $\Delta\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{k}_{	ext{exc}} - \mathbf{k}_{	ext{scat}}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the measured signal is proportional to the local microwave power and utilizes the quasi-magnetostatic approximation for field calculations.

**Figures summary.** Figures show experimental contrast at varying probe distances, FFTs revealing anomalous low-k components, and simulations confirming these components originate from the cross-term interference.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the failure of the direct eigenmode mapping assumption, then models the total field as a sum of interfering components, and finally uses simulations and experiments to isolate the interference term as the source of apparent zero-momentum signals.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Spatially resolved measurements of coherent waves are commonly read as direct maps of the underlying eigenmode spectrum. We show that this interpretation fails in near-field imaging of multimode spin-wave transport. Scanning nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry of yttrium iron garnet reveals pronounced apparent low-wave-vector signals at frequencies for which no propagating spin-wave mode exists. By tuning the probe-sample distance and modeling the anisotropic near-field response, we identify their origin as coherent mixing between directly excited Damon-Eshbach waves and defect- or transducer-scattered spin waves: the measured signal acquires spatial Fourier components at the difference wave vector $\mathbf{k}_{\mathrm{exc}}-\mathbf{k}_{\mathrm{scat}}$, which can vanish even though both constituent waves carry finite momentum. These results establish that near-field spectra of coherent excitations are interferometric field spectra rather than eigenmode maps, providing both a caution and a framework for identifying scattering processes in nanoscale magnonic devices.

</details>
